It differs from the standard smoothness loss by using image intensity gradients as edge-aware weights [S2].

The evidence explicitly defines the smoothing term TV_normal using an exponential function of the absolute difference in image intensity (|I_{i,j} - I_{i-1,j}| and |I_{i,j} - I_{i,j-1}|). In the context of total variation loss, these exponential terms act as weights that reduce the penalty for differences in normal vectors when there is a large difference in image intensity (i.e., at edges). This confirms that the loss uses image intensity gradients (or differences) as edge-aware weights, distinguishing it from a standard smoothness loss which typically does not condition on image intensity.

l_scale += min_idx  # ||argmin(s_i)||_1 for a scalar index is the index itself [S1]

The claim states that `l_scale += min_idx` corresponds to `||argmin(s_i)||_1` and that for a scalar index, the L1 norm is the index itself. The evidence explicitly defines the scale loss as `L_scale = sum_i ||argmin(s_i)||_1`. In the context of the paper, `s_i` is a vector `(s1, s2, s3)`, and `argmin(s_i)` returns the index (0, 1, or 2) corresponding to the minimum scaling factor. The notation `||...||_1` applied to a scalar index (which is what `argmin` returns in this discrete context) is mathematically equivalent to the index value itself (since the L1 norm of a scalar is its absolute value, and indices are non-negative). Therefore, the code snippet `l_scale += min_idx` accurately implements the mathematical formula provided in the evidence.
